newsitem.title: UK: Will UK monetary committee speak with one voice?.
newsitem.headline: Will UK monetary committee speak with one voice?.

text.p: Among the intriguing questions surrounding the new monetary policy committee which Britain's Labour government plans to put in charge of interest rates is whether or not it will speak in public with one voice.

Will its members become high-profile figures in their own right, capable of unsettling financial markets with their personal views on policy, like members of Germany's Bundesbank Council or the U.S. Federal Open Markets Committee? Or will Britain's traditions of official secrecy force them to keep their views to themselves?

New Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Gordon Brown astounded financial markets on Tuesday by announcing that he would cede the freedom to set interest rates to a nine-member committee at the Bank of England.
Brown will name four outsiders to join Bank Governor Eddie George and other senior staff on the committee, as well as appointing a second deputy governor.
Minutes of their monthly meetings will be published within six weeks and any votes taken will be recorded.
Details of the three-year contracts of the four outside members have not been spelled out, but the assumption at the Bank of England appears to be that discretion will be the order of the day.
"They will be employees of the Bank of England," a Bank official said. "We do have a confidentiality requirement at the Bank."
However, City economists, including some former advisers to the Treasury, say committee members could become important figures in their own right.

"I think the procedure ought to be that one doesn't express one's views between the meetings," said a former "Wise Man" -- a member of the independent panel of economic advisers which advised former Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.

"What we did on the Treasury panel was that anyone could say what they liked whenever they liked, but you could never disclose what was happening on the panel itself," said the economist, who asked not be named. "That worked all right."

Martin Weale, director of the National Institute of Economic and Social Research and another former "Wise Man," said that if committee members make public statements, there is a risk of them occasionally unsettling markets.

"It remains to be seen whether they will be bound by confidentiality," he said. "But they will be in a different position from Bundesbank officials because they will be working for the Bank of England."

Members of Britain's monetary committee will certainly lack the power base in regional central banks that makes individual members of the Bundesbank council or the U.S. Federal Open Market Committee powerful figures.
But interest in the views of the people actually responsible for framing monetary policy will be intense.

"They will be asked their opinions," said Ruth Lea, head of the policy unit at the Institute of Directors. "What are they going to do -- say nothing.? My feeling is they will speak and the runes will be read."
She believes much will depend on the types of contracts the four outside committee members are given.
Brown's letter to Bank Governor Eddie George said only that they would be appointed for a three-year term.
"They will be recognised experts," Brown wrote. "They will be allowed to engage, with the Chancellor's approval, in other activities which do not give rise to a conflict of interest."
Lea says that if the outside committee members have full-time or virtually full-time jobs elsewhere, it will be more difficult to rein them in.
"If they are relatively public figures, they will be asked their opinions quite a lot. People will be interested in what they think," she said.
Some economists say that outside experts brought into the Bank will in time succumb to the received wisdom of George and his senior colleagues, but the former Wise Men disagree.
"My guess is they will remain independent figures," one said.

Weale said that, in his experience, the Bank was good at "taking an objective view and looking at things from different sides." "I don't think there is a question of the newcomers going native or anything like that," he said.
His overall verdict on Brown's radical shake-up of monetary policy is lukewarm.
"It perhaps increases the risk that we will see poor coordination between fiscal and monetary policy. I think that is a very real downside," he said.
